idiom_name: Rails Authentication concern + has_secure_password session guard
implementation_notes: Rails 8's built-in authentication generator is the framework-native realization: User.has_secure_password stores a bcrypt password hash, SessionsController calls User.authenticate_by for credential verification, and the Authentication concern included by ApplicationController runs before_action :require_authentication. resume_session loads the signed session cookie into Current.session, while allow_unauthenticated_access marks explicit public actions; start_new_session_for creates the authenticated session after a successful comparison. Devise/Warden's authenticate_user! is a valid alternative, but it is not Rails core; hand-written Rack middleware is warranted only on a stack without controller concerns.
code_sketch:
class User < ApplicationRecord
  has_secure_password
end

class ApplicationController < ActionController::Base
  include Authentication                    # before_action :require_authentication
  allow_unauthenticated_access only: :health
end

class SessionsController < ApplicationController
  allow_unauthenticated_access only: :create
  def create
    if user = User.authenticate_by(params.permit(:email_address, :password))
      start_new_session_for(user)            # new server-side session + signed cookie
      redirect_to after_authentication_url
    else
      redirect_to new_session_url, alert: "Try another email address or password."
    end
  end
end
pitfalls: Omitting include Authentication (or broadly skipping require_authentication) removes the controller checkpoint, so every action is anonymous or an accidental public exception; include it in the common controller and allow only deliberate public actions.

Putting a raw password or a reusable pre-login session ID in the session leaks credentials or enables fixation; authenticate_by against the bcrypt hash, create a new server-side session after success, and expire/rotate identifiers on privilege changes.
